title: Real-Time Chat Application
shortDescription: A real-time messaging platform built with React, Node.js, Express, MongoDB and Socket.IO.
description: A messaging application where two people can talk with no page refresh anywhere in the flow. Socket.IO carries messages, presence and typing state over a single connection, while REST endpoints handle authentication and message history. A Gemini-backed assistant can draft replies and translate incoming messages.
features: Responsive layout down to small phones

details.overview: A chat platform for one-to-one conversations, built to understand how stateful real-time systems differ from ordinary request/response web apps.
details.problem: Polling an API for new messages is simple to write but wastes requests, adds latency and makes presence and typing indicators impractical. I wanted a version where the server pushes instead.
details.solution: A persistent Socket.IO connection per signed-in user, with rooms keyed by conversation. Messages are written to MongoDB and emitted to the room in the same handler, so history and live delivery never diverge. REST handles login, contact lists and paginated history; sockets handle everything that changes second to second.
details.architecture: React client (Vite) <-> Express REST API for auth and history, and a Socket.IO channel for messages, presence and typing. Mongoose models for User, Conversation and Message. JWT is verified in the Socket.IO handshake so a socket can never outlive its session.
challenges: Keeping presence accurate when a browser tab closes without a clean disconnect
Preventing duplicate messages when a client reconnects mid-send
Debouncing typing events so they do not flood the socket
learned: How to authenticate a socket handshake rather than a request
Why optimistic UI needs a server-assigned message id to reconcile against
That real-time features are mostly a state-synchronisation problem, not a transport problem

title: NexaCart
shortDescription: A full-stack e-commerce platform with separate customer and admin applications over one API.
description: An online store split into three deployable pieces: a customer storefront, an admin dashboard, and the Express API both talk to. Payments run through Razorpay, images through Cloudinary, and sign-in supports both email/password and Google.

details.overview: A working storefront with the parts that usually get skipped in tutorial e-commerce: real payment flow, real image hosting, and an admin surface that is a separate application rather than a hidden route.
details.problem: Most student e-commerce projects stop at a product grid and a fake checkout. I wanted the money path and the operations path to actually exist, because those are where the interesting constraints are.
details.solution: Three applications against one API. The customer app handles browsing, cart and checkout. The admin app handles catalogue and orders behind a role check. The API owns all business rules, so neither client can be trusted with pricing or order state.
details.architecture: Customer app (React) and admin app (React) both call the Express API. MongoDB stores users, products, carts and orders. Firebase handles Google sign-in and hands the API a verified token. Razorpay order creation happens server-side and the payment signature is verified server-side before an order is marked paid. Cloudinary receives uploads via a signed request.
challenges: Verifying the Razorpay payment signature on the server so a client cannot fake a paid order
Reconciling a guest cart with a user cart at sign-in
Keeping one shared API contract usable by two very different frontends
learned: Never let the client send the price — recompute totals from the database at checkout
How to sign and verify a third-party payment callback
That an admin app is a product with its own users, not an afterthought

title: CoretexAI
shortDescription: An AI platform that puts chat, retrieval and tool-using agents behind one interface.
description: An in-progress MERN application exploring multi-agent AI workflows: a chat interface backed by LangGraph, retrieval over a Qdrant vector store, and streaming responses. Built to learn how agent orchestration, caching and containerised deployment fit together.

details.overview: My current long-running project and the one I am learning the most from. It is under active development — the sections below describe what is built and what is still in progress.
details.problem: Single-prompt LLM calls fall over as soon as a task needs several steps, external data or a tool. I wanted to build the orchestration layer myself rather than treat it as a black box.
details.solution: A LangGraph state machine routes a request to the right agent, which can call tools, query the vector store, or hand back to the planner. Responses stream to the client token by token so long chains stay usable. Redis caches embeddings and holds job state between steps.
details.architecture: React + Redux Toolkit client <-> Express API. LangGraph orchestrates agents; Qdrant stores document embeddings for retrieval; Redis caches and tracks long-running jobs; MongoDB stores users, conversations and document metadata. Docker images are built for both services and deployed to AWS.
challenges: Streaming partial responses through an Express route without buffering
Chunking documents so retrieval returns relevant context rather than noise
Keeping agent state consistent when a step fails halfway through
learned: How a graph-based agent runtime differs from a simple prompt chain
That retrieval quality is mostly a chunking and embedding problem
How to containerise a multi-service application for deployment

title: Inventory Management System
shortDescription: A desktop inventory and billing system for products, suppliers, categories and staff operations.
description: A Python desktop application for running a small shop's back office: product and supplier records, categories, billing, and separate admin and employee accounts with an email OTP password reset.

details.overview: A desktop CRUD application built before I moved to web development. It is the project where I first had to think about database schema design rather than just queries.
details.problem: A small shop tracking stock and bills on paper has no way to look up what was sold, what is low, or which supplier a product came from.
details.solution: A Tkinter interface over a normalised MySQL schema, with two account types: admins manage the catalogue and staff, employees handle billing. Password reset goes through a one-time code sent by email rather than a security question.
details.architecture: Tkinter views call a data-access layer that owns every SQL statement, so the UI never builds queries itself. MySQL holds products, categories, suppliers, employees and bills with foreign keys between them.
challenges: Designing the schema so deleting a supplier does not orphan its products
Keeping the UI responsive while sending the OTP email
Validating input at the boundary rather than trusting form fields
learned: Why a data-access layer is worth writing even in a small app
How foreign keys and cascade rules shape what the UI can safely offer

title: Secure Login System
shortDescription: A web application for authentication, user information management and controlled file access.
description: A FOSSEE task built around access control: authenticated users, protected routes, role-based permissions, and files that only the right role can download.

details.overview: A focused project about one thing: making sure a request can only reach what its owner is allowed to reach.
details.problem: Hiding a link in the UI is not access control. A file endpoint has to check the requester's role on every request, not once at login.
details.solution: JWT-authenticated sessions, a role stored against each user, and middleware that authorises per route and per file rather than per page. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt and never returned by any query.
details.architecture: Express API with PostgreSQL. Auth middleware verifies the token, a role guard runs after it, and file downloads are streamed only after an ownership and role check passes.
challenges: Making authorisation checks impossible to skip by adding them as middleware rather than inline
Handling token expiry without logging people out mid-task
Serving files without exposing a path that could be walked
learned: The difference between authentication and authorisation in practice
Why role checks belong on the server route, never in the frontend router
How to design SQL schema around permissions
